title: DAVIDAU DELETED MY POST AND BANNED ME FOR ASKING ABOUT BENCHMARKS — HERE IS THE FULL ANALYSIS (9B + 27B + 390 MODELS)
gist: A Hugging Face user documents that DavidAU — a prolific fine-tuner with roughly 390 model repos and millions of downloads — markets every model on the same seven saturated 2018-2019 benchmarks while never running a single modern one, then deleted a discussion asking for SWE-bench scores and banned the author from all repositories. The post's core evidence is that the flagship 'Fusion-711' intelligence claim rests on a 6.4-point ARC-C gain over base Qwen 3.6 27B, on a benchmark a 2024 Snowflake paper showed swings 29 points purely from evaluation formatting.

insights.claim: A Hugging Face model publisher deleted rather than closed a discussion requesting modern benchmark scores and then blocked the requester from interacting with any of his 390-plus repositories, removing the community's only feedback channel.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Model hubs have no separation between publisher and moderator of the evidence about a model, so download counts and discussion sentiment are publisher-curated metrics, not independent signal.
insights.quote: He deleted it and then blocked me from interacting with any of his repositories
insights.locator: I posted a discussion on the Qwen3.6-27B-Fable-Fusion-711 model page

insights.claim: The alleged moderation pattern is systematic rather than isolated: closing a discussion where a user reported a coding failure, ignoring a direct SWE-bench request, pinning positive threads, and deleting critical analysis.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A reusable due-diligence heuristic: check whether a publisher's discussion tab contains unresolved criticism — an all-positive tab on a high-download repo is a red flag, not a green one.
insights.quote: The pattern is clear: close, ignore, delete, ban.
insights.locator: This is the same person who

insights.claim: When asked for real benchmark results the publisher's documented answer was 'Trust me bro, it's the best', a response the community quoted back in the discussion threads.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Absence of verifiable evaluation is the norm rather than the exception in the community fine-tune tier — a structural quality gap that professional evaluation services could monetize.
insights.quote: Q: 'Would you mind to share the real benchmark results please?' A: 'Trust me bro, it's the best.'

insights.claim: Every model in a 390-plus repo catalog is evaluated on the identical seven benchmarks — ARC-C, ARC-E, BOOLQ, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA and Winogrande — all published between 2018 and 2019 and all designed for the BERT/GPT-2 era.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Benchmark choice is a marketing decision at the fine-tune tier; any model card citing only pre-2020 multiple-choice benchmarks should be treated as unevaluated.
insights.quote: All from 2018-2019. All designed for the BERT/GPT-2 era.

insights.claim: The entire 'zone of intelligence' claim for the flagship 27B model rests on a single-benchmark move from base Qwen 3.6 27B's ARC-C 0.647 to the fine-tune's 0.711 — a 6.4-point gain on one saturated test that also supplies the model's name.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A named-after-the-metric product is a tell that the metric was the goal; expect the gain not to transfer to agentic or coding workloads that actually drive enterprise value.
insights.quote: So the entire "zone of intelligence" claim is built on a 6.4% improvement on a single saturated benchmark.

insights.claim: The BOOLQ score is unchanged between fine-tune and base on both model sizes (0.895 on the 9B, 0.910 on the 27B), showing zero improvement on one of the seven benchmarks used to justify the intelligence claims.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Flat scores on saturated tests are evidence of ceiling effects, not of parity — a reminder to check whether a benchmark can still move before treating it as a comparison.
insights.quote: BOOLQ is identical on both models (0.895 = 0.895 on 9B, 0.910 = 0.910 on 27B). Zero improvement.

insights.claim: The scaled-up 40B expansion scored worse on the defining metric, with ARC-C dropping from 0.711 to 0.695 while the model card still claimed operation at OpenAI, Claude and Gemini levels.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Marketing claims persisting through a measured regression is the clearest available evidence that the published numbers do not drive the messaging.
insights.quote: The 40B is worse on the one benchmark that supposedly defines "intelligence."

insights.claim: Frontier labs do not compete on ARC-C at all — they neither report it nor market around it, competing instead on SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, GPQA Diamond, LiveCodeBench, AIME and HMMT.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: The benchmark suite a vendor chooses reveals which market it is really competing in; agentic and coding benchmarks are now the only ones with commercial signal.
insights.quote: OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini do not compete on ARC-C. They don't report it. They don't market around it.
insights.locator: OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini do not compete

themes.theme: The research that invalidates ARC-C as a discriminator

insights.claim: A 2024 Snowflake AI Research paper (Borchmann, arXiv:2412.17758) showed Llama 3.1 70B's ARC-C accuracy jumped from 64% to 93% simply by presenting all answer options at once, a 29-point swing from evaluation formatting alone.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Multiple-choice benchmark scores are not comparable across harnesses, so any leaderboard mixing evaluation setups is measuring configuration rather than capability.
insights.quote: ARC-C accuracy jumped from 64% to 93% — a 29-point swing just from changing the format
insights.locator: THE RESEARCH THAT INVALIDATES THE ARC-C CLAIM

insights.claim: 31% of ARC-C questions are described as hardly answerable in separation because they require comparing options, yet are conventionally evaluated without showing all choices.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A concrete mechanism for why legacy benchmark deltas are noise, useful for discounting any small-model 'beats frontier' claim built on them.
insights.quote: 31% of ARC-C questions are "hardly answerable in separation"

insights.claim: OpenBookQA moved from 48% to 89% under corrected evaluation, meaning it is essentially solved and any remaining score differences between models are evaluation artifacts.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Several benchmarks still cited in model cards carry zero discriminating information; treat their appearance as a dating signal for the evaluation stack.
insights.quote: OpenBookQA went from 48% to 89% with correct evaluation

insights.claim: The cited paper's conclusion is that ARC-Challenge's perceived difficulty was primarily an artifact of the evaluation method rather than the complexity of the tasks themselves.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Reinforces that eval-harness configuration is the dominant variable in reported small-model results — a reason to demand harness disclosure before acting on any benchmark claim.
insights.quote: The previously perceived difficulty was primarily an artifact of the evaluation method rather than the tasks' complexity

themes.theme: The evaluation gap versus base-model disclosure

insights.claim: The base model reports a full modern suite the fine-tune never touches: Qwen 3.6 27B publishes SWE-bench Verified 77.2, SWE-bench Pro 53.5, Terminal-Bench 2.0 59.3, GPQA Diamond 87.8, MMLU-Pro 86.2, LiveCodeBench v6 83.9, AIME26 94.1 and HMMT Feb 26 84.3.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A useful reference line for where open 27B-class models actually sit on agentic coding as of mid-2026 — 77.2 on SWE-bench Verified is the number to benchmark competitors against.

insights.claim: Qwen 3.5 9B's published card reports MMLU-Pro 82.5, GPQA Diamond 81.7, LiveCodeBench v6 65.6, BFCL-V4 66.1, TAU2-Bench 79.1 and IFEval 91.5, but also weak agentic scores of OSWorld-Verified 41.8, AndroidWorld 57.8 and DeepPlanning 18.0.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Even strong small models remain weak on OS-agent and long-horizon planning benchmarks, which is where the real capability gap — and therefore the investment opportunity — still sits.

insights.claim: The fine-tuner copy-pastes the entire official Qwen 3.5 9B model card, showing 25-plus modern benchmarks the base model reports, into his own README while testing his fine-tune on none of them.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Inherited model-card content lets derivative publishers borrow base-model credibility; readers should verify which numbers were actually measured on the artifact being downloaded.
insights.quote: He includes the card showing what the base model can do on SWE-bench, GPQA, LiveCodeBench, BFCL, TAU2-Bench — and then tests his fine-tune on none of them.

insights.claim: Fine-tuning can raise legacy benchmark scores while silently degrading real capabilities, so a fine-tune reporting only the seven benchmarks it improved leaves function calling, agentic performance, instruction following and PhD-level reasoning entirely unmeasured.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Selective benchmark reporting is a structural risk for anyone deploying community fine-tunes into agentic pipelines, where the unreported capabilities are precisely the ones that matter.
insights.quote: When you train a model to perform better on specific benchmarks, you can easily degrade its performance on other tasks — especially agentic ones.

insights.claim: The fine-tuner's substitute for standardized evaluation is a 'human testing' claim with no documented prompts, methodology, reproducibility or published results — which the author characterises as anecdote.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Vibes-based evaluation is widespread across the open fine-tune ecosystem; standardized third-party evaluation of community models is an underserved need.
insights.quote: "Human testing" with no methodology, no documented prompts, no reproducibility, and no published results is just anecdote.

themes.theme: Scale of distribution versus scale of verification

insights.claim: The 9B model records 419,415 downloads per month and the 27B model over 1.6 million downloads with 25,000-plus monthly on GGUF and 1,500-plus likes, all on the strength of 2018-era science-quiz scores.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Download volume on model hubs is driven by naming, marketing and social hype rather than measured quality — so hub download counts are a poor proxy for real-world model adoption or usage value.

insights.claim: The catalog spans five collections — 284 models in the main collection, 135 dark/evil/corrupt, 130 heretic uncensored, 65 spanning 0.8B to 87B, and 17 Qwen 3.6 fine-tunes — totalling roughly 390 unique repos with combined downloads in the millions.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A single individual can occupy a meaningful share of hub distribution, meaning hub-level quality signals are highly concentrated and easily distorted by one prolific publisher.
insights.quote: 390+ models. Same 7 saturated benchmarks. Every. Single. Time.

themes.theme: GGUF quantization quality claims without verification

insights.claim: Custom quantization methods branded NEO IMATRIX, DI-MATRIX and TRI-MATRIX are shipped with no published calibration data, no perplexity measurements and no comparison against standard imatrix, while the card claims NEO IMATRIX improves accuracy by an additional 2-4% over normal GGUFs.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Quantization quality is the least-verified layer of the local-inference stack, and perplexity-versus-F16 comparison is the cheap test that would settle such claims.
insights.quote: 2-4% improvement is a significant claim with zero evidence.
insights.locator: Custom quantization methods with no verification

insights.claim: Legacy quantization formats Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0 and Q5_1 use uniform scalar quantization inferior to K-quants, with Q4_0 carrying roughly 5x the perplexity error of Q4_K_M at nearly identical file size, yet legacy quants are used without explanation.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable quality criterion for anyone sourcing local model weights: reject legacy quants when K-quants of similar size exist.
insights.quote: Q4_0 has roughly 5x the perplexity error of Q4_K_M at nearly identical file size

insights.claim: IQ quants without a proper model-specific imatrix are usually worse than the equivalent K-quant, and double quantization can severely reduce quality to the point that llama.cpp refuses it by default.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: The tooling's own defaults encode quality guardrails, so any publisher overriding llama.cpp defaults owes an evidence-backed justification.
insights.quote: Double quantization "can severely reduce quality" — llama.cpp refuses this by default
insights.locator: IQ quants without a proper model-specific imatrix

insights.claim: Users independently reported quality failures including gibberish output from a GPT-OSS 20B variant, a 120B variant spitting gibberish 20% of the time, and looping tool calls in Hermes on the 27B model.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Looping tool calls and gibberish are exactly the agentic failure modes legacy benchmarks cannot detect, confirming the reported-versus-real capability gap.
insights.quote: spitting gibberish 20% of the time

insights.claim: The publisher's own explanation for gibberish output was that Q8 quants are 'padded', implying that the highest standard quantization level has reduced performance specifically on his models.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: An explanation that inverts the normal quality-versus-size relationship is itself a diagnostic that something is wrong upstream in the conversion pipeline.
insights.quote: "Q8s are 'padded'; reducing performance."

insights.claim: The critiqued model cards provide zero reproducibility — no eval scripts, prompts, harness config, few-shot setup, temperature or sampling parameters — offering only a bar chart with no methodology.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Reproducibility disclosure is the cheapest available filter for separating credible open-model releases from marketing, and it is fully observable before download.
insights.quote: Zero reproducibility in either model card. No eval scripts. No prompts. No harness config.

insights.claim: The contrast case is the official Qwen 3.6 27B card, which publishes structured sections, 25-plus benchmark tables, evaluation methodology footnotes covering harness, temperature, top_p, context window and number of runs, architecture specs, reproducible quickstart code and a BibTeX citation.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Qwen is setting the documentation standard for open-weight releases, which raises the disclosure bar every other open-model publisher will be judged against.
insights.quote: The Qwen 3.6 card tells you exactly how each benchmark was run. These cards tell you to trust a bar chart.
insights.locator: Compare with the Qwen 3.6 27B official model card

insights.claim: Presentation itself signals quality: the 9B README runs 145 KB against a typical 2-10 KB model card, padded with marketing superlatives, a copy-pasted base-model card, four long example generations and a 4.22 MB GIF.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Document bloat and 68-to-80-character model names are cheap, observable proxies for the absence of evaluation discipline underneath.
insights.quote: The 9B README is 145 KB. Most model cards are 2-10 KB.

insights.claim: The author's stated position is not that the models are bad but that the evidence provided makes their quality unknowable, since it consists only of unreliable 2018 benchmarks presented alongside marketing language with zero modern coverage or GGUF quality verification.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Frames the actionable gap as an information problem rather than a quality verdict — the opportunity is independent evaluation infrastructure for the community model tier.
insights.quote: I'm not saying these models are bad. I genuinely don't know — and that's the problem.

insights.claim: A commenter reports independently quantizing the same 27B model and finding that 16-bit output is a waste of model size while low quants perform well on wiki text, offering a rare piece of third-party verification in the thread.
insights.speaker: DedeProGames
insights.so_what: Independent re-quantization by community members is currently the only functioning verification mechanism on model hubs, and it is entirely voluntary and unfunded.
insights.quote: Output in 16-bit is just waste of model size.
